neighbours.label: a character's unquoted thought in fiction: where narration slips into their inner voice ('Oh no, not today.', 'Too late, he told himself')
fire: Anna saw him across the station and froze. Oh no, not today. I look terrible!
He put the phone down and stared at the wall. Too late now, he told himself, and went upstairs.
Priya read the note twice. Of course. He had known all along. How had she missed it?
The engine coughed and died. Damn it. I knew I should have filled the tank.
She folded the last shirt and shut the case. Three more weeks, she thought, and turned off the light.
Tom watched the boat pull away. Stupid, he thought, so stupid, even for him.
Lena heard the key in the lock. Not yet. Please, not yet. I need more time.
The captain looked over the empty deck. Well, that settled it. They would sail at dawn.
quiet: Anna saw him across the station and waved, then picked up her bag and walked over to the ticket office.
He put the phone down, crossed the room, and went upstairs to fetch his coat from the hall closet.
Priya read the note twice, signed it at the bottom, and passed it to the clerk behind the counter.
The engine coughed and started, and the old truck rolled slowly down the hill toward the village.
She folded the last shirt, shut the case, turned off the light, and carried the luggage to the car.
Tom watched the boat pull away from the dock while the gulls circled above the harbor wall.
Lena heard the key in the lock and opened the door for the man who delivered the mail.
The captain walked over the empty deck and gave the crew their orders for the morning tide.

notes: Peaks on punctuation or the first token inside the thought. Probes: 0.42-0.77 with a lead-in sentence, under 0.02 for outward narration. A bare thought with no narrative lead-in was weaker (0.07-0.16).
